name: Arizona

notes: Groceries: voters approved Proposition 316 on November 3, 2026, 1,263,335 for and 794,867 against (Secretary of State, unofficial count of November 4; the state canvass is to come). From June 30, 2027 it freezes city food taxes of 2% or more, lets lower ones rise only by a vote and only to 2%, and requires a vote for new ones (capped at 2%); no adoption or increase may take effect in the 24 months before June 30, 2027, and it applies back to January 1, 2025. Current city food rates are used here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and spirits are taxed at the full rate, on top of the state luxury tax paid by distributors ($3 a gallon on spirits, 84 cents on wine, 16 cents on beer), which is left out here.
Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of the $2.00-a-pack cigarette tax and the tax on other tobacco products, left out here. No state tax on vapor products was found.
Barber and beauty services: personal services such as haircuts aren't taxed: no TPT classification covers them (no ADOR statement found that says so directly).
Laundry and dry cleaning services aren't taxed: no TPT classification covers them (no ADOR statement found that says so directly).
Motor fuel is exempt from TPT and taxed by the gallon instead: 18 cents for gasoline, left out here. A 2026 bill for a fuel tax holiday (HB 2400) was not enacted.
Repair labor billed separately from parts is not taxed.
Diapers, menstrual products and other hygiene products are taxed at the full rate; Arizona has no sales tax holiday.
Hotel stays pay city hotel taxes and, in Maricopa and Pima counties, county lodging taxes, which are not counted here.
gaps: Arizona taxes sellers (transaction privilege tax) rather than buyers; rates are passed on like a sales tax.

Groceries (food for home consumption) carry no state or county tax; each city taxes them at its own rate, which is used here, and 22 cities don't tax them (Bullhead City, Camp Verde, Flagstaff, Jerome, Kingman, Lake Havasu City, Marana, Mesa, Oro Valley, Parker, Phoenix, Quartzsite, Sahuarita, San Tan Valley, Sedona, South Tucson, Superior, Surprise, Tombstone, Tucson, Tusayan, Williams).

Restaurants and bars: 23 cities tax them at a different rate from other retail sales (Casa Grande, Chandler, Colorado City, Eloy, Flagstaff, Glendale, Goodyear, Guadalupe, Jerome, Kingman, Lake Havasu City, Page, Parker, Peoria, Pinetop-Lakeside, Quartzsite, Sierra Vista, South Tucson, Surprise, Tusayan, Williams, Winslow, Yuma); their restaurant rate is used for restaurants.

Places in two counties: in each census tract the city's rate is taken with the tract's county's, counted for the share of the tract's store jobs (jobs at restaurants, bars and hotels, for restaurants) located in the city: Apache Junction (Pinal County, Maricopa County); Hayden (Gila County, Pinal County); Marana (Pima County, Pinal County); Peoria (Maricopa County, Yavapai County); Queen Creek (Maricopa County, Pinal County); Sedona (Yavapai County, Coconino County); Wickenburg (Maricopa County, Yavapai County); Winkelman (Gila County, Pinal County).
Some cities tax the part of a single item's price above a set amount at a lower rate (Phoenix 2% above $14,338, for one; 29 cities in all); not counted.
Taxes on sales on tribal lands are not counted.
San Tan Valley incorporated after the 2024 Census place list; its rate is applied to the San Tan Valley CDP.

Local sales tax votes on November 3, 2026: by the county election offices' unofficial counts, Tempe's Proposition 424, Prescott Valley's Proposition 493, Yavapai County's Proposition 497 and Flagstaff's Proposition 404 failed and Tucson's zoo tax renewal (Proposition 422) passed; these and San Tan Valley's grocery tax from January 1, 2027, which the statewide Proposition 316 (approved) may bar, are noted on those pages. The rates here are ADOR's for November 1, 2026. Smaller towns' November measures weren't all checked.

0423620: Flagstaff voters rejected Proposition 404, a 0.5% sales tax for public safety from July 1, 2027 for 15 years (to June 30, 2042), not on groceries, which would have raised the city's rate from 2.486% to 2.986% (Coconino County's official title; City of Flagstaff, call of election), on November 3, 2026, 9,519 for and 11,028 against (Coconino County Elections, unofficial count of November 4, with ballots still being counted). The current rate is used here.
0457450: Prescott Valley voters rejected Proposition 493, a 0.5% sales tax for a pool and recreation center (as reported by KNAU), on November 3, 2026, 6,916 for and 12,355 against (Yavapai County Elections, unofficial count of November 4). The current rate is used here.
0464210: San Tan Valley, which incorporated in 2025, taxes food for home consumption at 2.25% from January 1, 2027 (Ordinance 2026-06; ADOR); groceries here are at 0% until then. Voters approved Proposition 316 on November 3, 2026 (Secretary of State, unofficial count of November 4): it bars a city food tax adopted without a vote, above 2% or in the 24 months before June 30, 2027, and applies back to January 1, 2025, so by its terms it may stop this one; the Department of Revenue hasn't said yet (rechecked November 6, 2026).
0473000: Tempe voters rejected Proposition 424, a 0.5% sales tax for public safety, transit and early childhood programs, not on food for home consumption (City of Tempe), on November 3, 2026, 17,395 for and 25,087 against (Maricopa County Elections, unofficial count of November 4, 3:40 a.m.). The current rate is used here.
0477000: Tucson voters approved Proposition 422, renewing the city's 0.1% zoo tax from January 1, 2028 to December 31, 2047 (City of Tucson), on November 3, 2026, 95,362 for and 36,784 against (Pima County Elections, unofficial count of November 4); the tax is in the current rate, which doesn't change.
04025: Yavapai County voters rejected Proposition 497, which would have raised the county jail district's sales tax by 0.25% (to 0.5%, as reported by KNAU) for 20 years from July 1, 2027 (Yavapai County Elections), on November 3, 2026, 47,168 for and 52,664 against (Yavapai County Elections, unofficial count of November 4). The current rate is used here.

local: a share of the growth in state sales tax collected in the district pays for development there

programs: Arizona has no enterprise zones (the program ended in 2011, as reported). Its two Military Reuse Zones aren't mapped: no boundaries are published (ADOR). Phoenix-Mesa Gateway's was first designated in 1996 and last renewed in 2015, and Phoenix-Goodyear's was designated in 2002 and renewed for ten years in 2017 (ADOR), so whether both are still in force wasn't confirmed. Its seven foreign-trade zones (60, 75, 139, 174, 219, 221 and 277) aren't mapped either: the federal Foreign-Trade Zones Board publishes their site lists and service-area maps, not map layers.

Business improvement districts are mapped for downtown Tucson (the city's 2022 layer). Not mapped (no official map found): the enhanced municipal services districts of downtown Phoenix, Tempe (downtown and Rio Salado), Mesa and Chandler, and Flagstaff's downtown district.

Tucson's Rio Nuevo district, where a share of state sales tax growth funds development, is drawn from the City of Tucson's current layer (October 2026). Other redevelopment and incentive areas aren't mapped: Phoenix's redevelopment areas (the City's published layer, from 2020, has 8 areas, its older Neighborhood Services map drew about 20, and the City's current list wasn't found), and Mesa's four redevelopment areas (its central business district, where GPLET abatements apply), which have no published layer.

warn: The 2020 census counted 83 people in Kaka, but the American Community Survey (2020–2024) estimates no households in the census tract its page is built from, so there is no resident spending to show here.
